text:
Heterotrophy categories and subcategories
Read from data/gene-lists/het_gene_reference.csv, the panel compiled by scripts/00_build_het_gene_reference.R. That script — not this document — resolves the awkward KEGG fields in the source lists ("K04624-K08424 (family range)", "K21348 (representative)", "Not in KEGG KO (non-orthologous)", ;-separated lists) and logs every unresolvable row to output-tables/00_het_gene_reference_unresolved.csv.
On the family-range rows ("K04624-K08424 (family range)"): the builder keeps both boundary ids as members and does not expand the range. KEGG ortholog numbers are assigned roughly sequentially rather than by family, so K04624–K08424 spans ~3,800 unrelated orthologs; expanding it would inject thousands of KOs with nothing to do with this gene set. Real family membership needs an actual KEGG lookup (the ko entry in the KEGG API), and the unresolved log records the range so that can be done deliberately.
Category and pathway assignment in the curated lists is still partial, so sets are kept down to MIN_SET_SIZE = 5 rather than the usual 15. Re-run scripts/00_build_het_gene_reference.R and then this document as that membership grows.


Code
het_ref <- read_csv(HET_REFERENCE, show_col_types = FALSE)

message(glue("{n_distinct(het_ref$ko_id)} heterotrophy KOs in the panel | ",
             "{n_distinct(het_ref$category)} categories, ",
             "{n_distinct(het_ref$subcategory)} subcategories"))


169 heterotrophy KOs in the panel | 3 categories, 25 subcategories

  filter(!is.na(subcategory)) |>

  (\(x) x[lengths(x) > 0])()

tibble(pathway = names(het_subcategory_sets),
       n       = lengths(het_subcategory_sets),
       source  = "het_subcategory") |>
  arrange(desc(n))

section: KEGG level-C pathways and Burns et al. 2018 trophic-mode families
text:
KEGG level-C pathways and Burns et al. 2018 trophic-mode families
Two outside sources, so the result does not depend on hand-picked membership (2026-10-21: approaches A and B).

kegg_level_c: every KEGG pathway map in Transport and catabolism, Signal transduction, Cell growth and death and Cell motility, with full KEGG membership. Prokaryote-only maps (two-component system, bacterial chemotaxis, bacterial flagellar assembly, Caulobacter cell cycle) are dropped in 00b. Many signaling maps share the same kinase core, so these sets overlap; read them as one family, not as independent results.
burns2018: protein families whose presence predicts phagocytosis, photosynthesis or prototrophy across 35 eukaryotic genomes (Burns et al. 2018, Nat Ecol Evol 2:697–704), mapped from UniProt representatives to KOs in 00b. Those families were chosen to predict gene content; here they are tested for a shift in expression between habitats, which is a different question from the one they were built for.

The protist experimental set (00b) is too small to clear MIN_SET_SIZE in this universe; 06b reports it KO by KO instead.

SKH:



Code
trophic_ref <- read_csv(TROPHIC_SETS, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(set_source %in% c("kegg_level_c", "burns2018"))

trophic_sets_by_source <- trophic_ref |>
  distinct(set_source, set_name, ko_id) |>
  (\(d) split(d, d$set_source))() |>
  map(\(d) split(d$ko_id, d$set_name))

kegg_level_c_sets <- trophic_sets_by_source$kegg_level_c %||% list()
burns_sets        <- trophic_sets_by_source$burns2018    %||% list()

if (!length(burns_sets)) {
  message("No burns2018 sets in ", TROPHIC_SETS, ": run scripts/00b_build_trophic_gene_sets.R ",
          "once with a network connection to build the UniProt -> KO cache.")
}

tibble(pathway = c(names(kegg_level_c_sets), names(burns_sets)),
       source  = rep(c("kegg_level_c", "burns2018"),
                     c(length(kegg_level_c_sets), length(burns_sets))),
       n       = c(lengths(kegg_level_c_sets), lengths(burns_sets)),
       n_ranked = map_int(c(kegg_level_c_sets, burns_sets), \(k) sum(k %in% names(ranks)))) |>
  arrange(source, desc(n_ranked))

title: 07 — fgsea: what’s enriched among vent-associated KOs
text:
Combine, tag by source
Size filtering happens on membership inside the ranked universe, not on raw membership. fgsea()’s own minSize applies to each set after intersecting it with stats, so a set with >= MIN_SET_SIZE KOs overall but fewer than that among the ranked KOs used to clear the filter here and then get dropped silently by fgsea(), which is what broke nrow(enrich) == length(all_sets) in the QC block (diagnosed and fixed 2026-09-27). Only the 06 class sets were ever immune, being built from ranks_df itself; the het and KEGG sets come from het_gene_reference.csv, which is not restricted to vent-associated KOs.
Multiple testing by family (>SKH: 2026-10-22). BH is applied within each family, not across every set: the original ten (span classes + curated heterotrophy subcategories + curated KEGG pathways) stay one family, as decided 2026-10-10, so adding the outside sources does not change their adjusted p-values. kegg_level_c and burns2018 are one family each.


Code
all_sets <- c(span_sets, het_subcategory_sets, kegg_sets, kegg_level_c_sets, burns_sets)
set_source <- rep(c("span_rank", "het_subcategory", "kegg_pathway", "kegg_level_c", "burns2018"),
                  c(length(span_sets), length(het_subcategory_sets),
                    length(kegg_sets), length(kegg_level_c_sets), length(burns_sets)))
names(set_source) <- names(all_sets)

# >SKH: BH family per source (see above)
set_family <- c(span_rank = "curated_panel", het_subcategory = "curated_panel",
                kegg_pathway = "curated_panel", kegg_level_c = "kegg_level_c",
                burns2018 = "burns2018")

# de-duplicate names across sources before filtering by size (fgsea keys on name)
names(all_sets) <- make.unique(names(all_sets))
names(set_source) <- names(all_sets)

size_in_universe <- lengths(map(all_sets, intersect, names(ranks)))
n_dropped        <- sum(size_in_universe < MIN_SET_SIZE)

all_sets   <- all_sets[size_in_universe >= MIN_SET_SIZE]
set_source <- set_source[names(all_sets)]

message(glue("{length(all_sets)} gene sets kept | {n_dropped} dropped: fewer than ",
             "{MIN_SET_SIZE} members among the {length(ranks)} ranked KOs"))


54 gene sets kept | 58 dropped: fewer than 5 members among the 853 ranked KOs


Code
tibble(source = set_source) |> count(source, name = "n_sets_kept")

title: 06 — Where and among which taxa vent functions are expressed
text:
For every vent-associated KO (detected in ≥ 30% of vent units, i.e. ≥ 4 of 13; the universe and habitat classes come from 05):

A. Where is it expressed? Vent units, vent fields, and whether it is also in background seawater (habitat_class from 05).
B. Among which taxa? The class-level (grain 4) taxa that carry it, counted at each rank of the curated taxonomy, and the deepest rank all contributing taxa share (span_rank). Average taxonomic distinctness (Δ+) tests whether the contributing taxa are more clustered than a random draw of the same size.
C. Where × who. Are field-restricted or vent-only functions carried by narrower lineages?
D. KEGG level-B composition of each span class: the blind, trend-reporting view.
E. Heterotrophy panel: the question-driven view. Which taxa carry each panel KO, and which taxa co-express the most heterotrophy subcategories.

Rules (config/params.yml, shared with 05, 05b and 07). Span rank and the taxon × KO contributing-taxon pairs are computed once, in 05b, and read here (2026-10-13); 06 adds field span, Δ+ and the heterotrophy view.

Detected in a unit: ≥ 1 scaledTPM and ≥ 10 per million of the unit’s retained expression.
Contributing taxon: a class-level taxon whose taxon × KO pair is detected in ≥ pair_min_units

vent units. Presence/absence only; these are compositional data, so a contributing taxon is a taxon whose share of that KO clears detection, not a count of cells.

Span rank (lowest common ancestor of the contributing taxa, conservative): class = one class-level taxon; phylum = one curated phylum; supergroup = one curated supergroup; cross-supergroup otherwise. A contributing taxon not resolved at a rank (an “(unres.)” class or an “-Unannotated” phylum) caps the span at the next coarser rank. Syndiniales is a phylum-level group, separate from Dinophyta (02 curation).
Δ+ (Clarke & Warwick 1998, J Appl Ecol 35:523–531; vegan::taxondive): mean rank distance between contributing-taxon pairs over supergroup / phylum / class. Its expected value does not depend on the number of contributing taxa, only its SD does, so dplus_z = (Δ+ − E[Δ+]) / SD compares KOs with different contributing-taxon counts on one scale. The conservative rule above is applied here too: unresolved classes and unannotated phyla never count as shared.

section: Which taxa carry each panel KO
text:
Which taxa carry each panel KO
Each cell is a contributing taxon’s share of that KO’s contributing-taxon expression at vents. Columns are vent-associated panel KOs grouped by subcategory; rows are contributing taxa grouped by curated group. The bar panel counts the subcategories each taxon carries (module completeness); its label is the taxon’s own mean share of vent expression, because a taxon with little expression has less chance of clearing detection for any KO.


Code
taxon_vent_share <- read_csv(TAXON_TABLE, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(cur_L4, cur_group, mean_share_vent)

het_carriers <- carriers |>
  filter(ko_id %in% het_ko$ko_id) |>
  mutate(share_of_ko = pair_tpm / sum(pair_tpm), .by = ko_id) |>
  left_join(taxon_vent_share, by = "cur_L4") |>
  mutate(taxon = taxon_label_unique(cur_L4))

het_taxon_ko <- het_carriers |>
  inner_join(het_long, by = "ko_id", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  select(cur_group, cur_L4, taxon, mean_share_vent, category, subcategory, ko_id, gene,
         pair_units, pair_tpm, share_of_ko)

# module completeness: panel subcategories (with >= 1 vent-associated KO) each taxon carries

  summarise(n_subcategories = n_distinct(subcategory), n_het_kos = n_distinct(ko_id),
            subcategories = paste(sort(unique(subcategory)), collapse = " | "),

title: 05 — Vent and non-vent signatures
text:
Who leads the vent and non-vent signatures: each class-level taxon’s share of expression and its occupancy, with the shares summed to supergroup (the 02 curated groups).
What dominant taxa comprise vent and non-vent: KEGG BRITE level-B composition of each habitat, and of each leading taxon.
Habitat classes for every KO and taxon (vent-only, vent-skewed, shared, non-vent-skewed, non-vent-only). The KO table is the hand-off to 06 and 07.
Rarefied sensitivity: the habitat classes recomputed at equal sequencing depth.

All of it is descriptive (occupancy and relative share).
Unit expression. Throughout this document, a unit’s expression is the scaledTPM that remains after Eukaryota-only and Opisthokonta assignments are removed, averaged over the unit’s replicates. Every proportion below is taken against that total.
Detection. A feature is detected in a sample unit when its unit total is ≥ detect_min_tpm (1) scaledTPM and ≥ detect_min_per_million (10) per million of that unit’s expression. scaledTPM carries library size (Soneson, Love & Robinson 2015, F1000Research 4:1521), and unit expression differs about 170-fold among units, so a TPM floor alone lets deep units detect more. The per-million floor protects deep units; the TPM floor protects shallow ones.
Occupancy. Associated with a habitat = detected in ≥ 30% of its units (occupancy_min_frac: ≥ 4 of 13 vent units, ≥ 2 of 6 non-vent units). A fraction rather than a count, so the bar is the same height in both habitats. Vent-only is strict: vent-associated and detected in no non-vent unit.
Shares are relative. A smaller share at vents means a smaller slice of protist expression, not fewer cells.

title: 05 — Vent and non-vent signatures
text:
Composition contrast: vent versus non-vent
Shares sum to 1 within a unit, so a larger share for one taxon forces smaller shares elsewhere. The contrast is therefore tested on robust-CLR values (zeros kept at 0, the 02/04 choice), and shares are used only for display. Three outputs:

Whole composition: PERMANOVA on rclr Euclidean (Aitchison) distance, vent versus non-vent, with a PERMDISP check; 13 vs. 6 units is unbalanced, so a dispersion difference can masquerade as a location difference.
Per taxon: Cliff’s delta (vent focal) on rclr, with a label-permutation max-T threshold across all features in the family, the same primary filter as 05.
Display: each unit’s share, zero where absent, with the habitat median.

Units, not libraries, are the replicates throughout.


Code
N_PERM_COMP <- 2000

composition_rclr <- function(ue, by_col) {
  ue |>
    select(unit, feature = all_of(by_col), tpm) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = feature, values_from = tpm, values_fill = 0) |>
    column_to_rownames("unit") |>
    as.matrix() |>
    rclr_transform()
}

compare_composition <- function(z, n_perm = N_PERM_COMP) {
  hab <- set_names(units$vent_bin, units$unit)[rownames(z)]
  observed <- contrast_ranks(z, hab, "Vent")
  null_max <- map_dbl(seq_len(n_perm), \(i)
    max(abs(contrast_ranks(z, set_names(sample(hab), names(hab)), "Vent")), na.rm = TRUE))
  tibble(feature = names(observed), cliffs_delta = observed,
         maxt_threshold = unname(quantile(null_max, 0.95))) |>
    # mutate(exceeds_maxt = abs(cliffs_delta) >= maxt_threshold)
    mutate(exceeds_maxt = abs(cliffs_delta) >= 0.5)
}

set.seed(params$seed)
z_group <- composition_rclr(group_unit, "cur_group")
z_taxon <- composition_rclr(tax_unit, "cur_L4")

# whole composition: PERMANOVA + PERMDISP on rclr Euclidean distance
composition_permanova <- imap_dfr(list(curated_group = z_group, class_level = z_taxon), \(z, grain) {
  meta <- tibble(unit = rownames(z)) |> left_join(units, by = "unit")
  d <- vegan::vegdist(z, method = "euclidean")
  perm <- vegan::adonis2(d ~ vent_bin, data = meta, permutations = 9999)
  disp <- vegan::permutest(vegan::betadisper(d, meta$vent_bin), permutations = 9999)
  tibble(grain, n_features = ncol(z), R2 = perm$R2[1], p = perm$`Pr(>F)`[1],
         dispersion_p = disp$tab$`Pr(>F)`[1])
})

title: 05 — Vent and non-vent signatures
section: Alternative view: same lineage or different lineages?
text:
Alternative view: same lineage or different lineages?
For each KEGG level-B category, the vent minus non-vent difference in its share of mapped expression is split into two parts (a midpoint shift-share decomposition, summed over class-level taxa):

Same lineage, different expression: each lineage expresses the category at a different share of its own expression in the two habitats.
Different lineages lead: the lineages that carry the expression differ between habitats, so the category changes even if each lineage behaved the same.

The two parts add exactly to the difference, and the total is checked against kegg_by_habitat. Lineages absent from one habitat contribute only to the second part.


Code
# lineage grain for the decomposition: "cur_L4" (class-level taxa) or "cur_group" (supergroups)
lineage_col <- "cur_L4"

n_hab <- count(units, vent_bin, name = "n_units")

# mean over ALL units of a habitat (absent = 0) of each lineage x category share of mapped expression
shift_mass <- unit_expression(kegg_long, c(lineage_col, "description")) |>
  select(unit, vent_bin, lineage = all_of(lineage_col), description, share) |>
  summarise(mass = sum(share), .by = c(vent_bin, lineage, description)) |>
  left_join(n_hab, by = "vent_bin") |>
  mutate(mass = mass / n_units) |>
  select(-n_units)

shift_wide <- shift_mass |>
  complete(vent_bin, lineage, description, fill = list(mass = 0)) |>
  mutate(w = sum(mass), .by = c(vent_bin, lineage)) |>                 # lineage share of mapped expression
  mutate(p = if_else(w > 0, mass / w, NA_real_)) |>                     # category profile within lineage
  pivot_wider(names_from = vent_bin, values_from = c(w, p, mass)) |>
  mutate(p_vent    = coalesce(p_Vent, `p_Non-vent`),                    # absent habitat: borrow the other profile
         p_nonvent = coalesce(`p_Non-vent`, p_Vent),
         within      = (w_Vent + `w_Non-vent`) / 2 * (p_vent - p_nonvent),
         composition = (w_Vent - `w_Non-vent`) * (p_vent + p_nonvent) / 2,
         delta       = mass_Vent - `mass_Non-vent`)

shift_decomp <- shift_wide |>
  summarise(within_lineage = sum(within), composition = sum(composition), delta = sum(delta),
            .by = description)

# the two parts must add to the difference, and the difference must match kegg_by_habitat
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(shift_decomp$within_lineage + shift_decomp$composition, shift_decomp$delta)))
shift_check <- shift_decomp |>
  left_join(transmute(kegg_by_habitat, description, ref = mean_share_Vent - `mean_share_Non-vent`),
            by = "description")
stopifnot(max(abs(shift_check$delta - shift_check$ref)) < 1e-8)

shift_decomp |>
  arrange(desc(abs(delta))) |>
  mutate(across(c(within_lineage, composition, delta), \(x) round(100 * x, 2)))

title: 05 — Vent and non-vent signatures
section: Alternative view: enrichment in vent-associated KOs
text:
Alternative view: enrichment in vent-associated KOs
The five habitat classes are merged into three groups: vent-associated (vent-only + vent-skewed), shared, and non-vent-associated (non-vent-only + non-vent-skewed). For each KEGG level-B category, observed KOs in a group are compared with the number expected if KOs fell into groups at random (all mapped, detected KOs as the background).

Fill is log2(observed / expected), with a 0.5 pseudocount. Red = over-represented, blue = under-represented.
Dot size is the number of KOs in that category and group (no dot = none).
* marks BH q <= 0.05 (Fisher’s exact test, one test per category and group, BH across all of them).
A KO placed in several categories counts once in each, so these are KO counts, not the fractional weights in the heatmap.
The vent-associated group is small (31 vent-only + 24 vent-skewed KOs, about 40 of them mapped to KEGG), so the tests have little power and are exploratory.
The non-vent-associated group largely reflects the deeper sequencing of non-vent units (see section 5), so read it as a contrast, not as habitat biology.

Superseded: this chord-distance heatmap is kept as the starting point for the diagnostics below. The figure version (euclidean_all) is rebuilt after them.

Diagnostics: why are most distances > 0.9?
The heatmap above uses the chord distance: decostand(method = "normalize") scales each sample to length 1, and the Euclidean distance between length-1 vectors runs from 0 (identical) to √2 ≈ 1.41 (no shared features) (Legendre & Gallagher 2001, Oecologia 129:271-280). Values near 1 or above can come from three different causes, and the steps below test each one:

Feature definition: the ko_PFAMs_GOs string splits one KO into many features, so samples share few of them.
Dominance: on raw TPM, a handful of very highly expressed transcripts make up most of each sample’s length.
The transform itself: compared on the same KO table, do normalize, hellinger and rclr (the transform 04-07 use; Gloor et al. 2017, Front Microbiol 8:2224) separate samples differently?

Positive control throughout: three units are true biological replicates with two libraries each (Von Damm_Vent_Ravelin2, Piccard_Vent_Lotsoshrimp, Gorda Ridge_Non-vent_Plume). A distance worth using puts those pairs among the closest pairs.

Step 0. Helper functions


Code
# Sparsity of a raw abundance matrix (rows = samples, cols = features)
feature_sparsity <- function(mat) {
  pres   <- mat > 0
  shared <- tcrossprod(pres)                       # features shared by each sample pair
  tibble(n_samples          = nrow(pres),
         n_features         = ncol(pres),
         prop_zero          = mean(!pres),         # share of empty cells
         prop_in_one_sample = mean(colSums(pres) == 1),
         median_shared      = median(shared[upper.tri(shared)]))
}

# Share of each sample's squared length that comes from its 10 largest features.
# This is how much of the chord distance those 10 features control.
top10_share <- function(mat) {
  apply(mat, 1, \(x) {
    x2 <- sort(x^2, decreasing = TRUE)
    sum(head(x2, 10)) / sum(x2)
  })
}

# Distance object -> one row per unique sample pair, flagged if the pair is a replicate pair
dist_pairs <- function(d) {
  m    <- as.matrix(d)
  unit <- set_names(str_remove(rownames(m), "\\|.*"), rownames(m))  # sample_id = raw_label|LIB|SAMPLEID
  as.data.frame(as.table(m)) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    rename(a = Var1, b = Var2, dist = Freq) |>
    mutate(across(c(a, b), as.character)) |>
    filter(a < b) |>                               # unique pairs, drop the diagonal
    mutate(pct            = percent_rank(dist),    # 0 = closest pair, 1 = farthest
           replicate_pair = unit[a] == unit[b])
}

# Spread and replicate control for one distance
dist_diagnostics <- function(d) {
  dist_pairs(d) |>
    summarise(n_pairs       = n(),
              min           = min(dist),
              median        = median(dist),
              max           = max(dist),
              cv            = sd(dist) / mean(dist),          # higher = more contrast between pairs
              replicate_pct = median(pct[replicate_pair]))    # low = replicates among the closest pairs
}

Step 3b. Is the rclr distance tracking KO richness?
In rclr, zeros stay 0, so a KO detected in one library and absent from another adds to their distance. Libraries that detect more KOs can end up far from the rest for that reason alone. Check whether each library’s mean distance tracks the number of KOs it detects, and whether the prevalence filter 04 uses (prevalence_filter(..., 4): a KO must be detected in at least 4 libraries) removes the dependence. Richness can also differ between habitats for real reasons, so the last chunk asks whether KO richness differs between vent and non-vent libraries.

    pivot_longer(c(a, b), values_to = "sample_id") |>
    group_by(sample_id) |>
    summarise(mean_dist = mean(dist)) |>
    left_join(enframe(rowSums(m$mat > 0), "sample_id", "n_kos"), by = "sample_id")

The distance used in the figures, chosen from the diagnostics above: KOs from the shared analysis set (the same table as 04-07), a KO kept if detected in at least 4 libraries (prevalence_filter(..., 4), as in 04), replicate libraries averaged to their biological unit, then rclr and Euclidean distance (robust Aitchison; Martino et al. 2019, mSystems 4:e00016-19). rclr was the only transform that placed true replicate libraries among the closest pairs (Step 3). plot_unit_distance <- function(d, title = NULL) {

  as.data.frame(as.table(m)) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    rename(X = Var1, Y = Var2, VALUE = Freq) |>
    mutate(across(c(X, Y), as.character)) |>

    geom_tile(color = "white", lwd = 0.75) +

# dat - input taxonomy matrix
# feat - input functional matrix
# label - add a label for matrix used
# Label grain - for the taxonomic level used. 
grain_fit <- function(dat, feat, label_matrix, label_grain) {
  tryCatch( # stop if error
    { # Build matrix for adonis2 fxn to run.
    bm <- build_matrix(dat, feat, min_tpm = 0, transform = params$transform)
    m  <- meta[match(labels(bm$dist), meta$sample_id), ]
    # PERMANOVA function
    perm <- run_permanova(bm$dist, m,
                          permutations = params$permutations,
                          seed = params$seed) |>
      filter(.data$term %in% c("vent_bin", "field")) |>
      select(term, R2, p)
    # dispersion check following permanova
    disp <- c(vent_bin = betadisper_check(bm$dist, m$vent_bin)$dispersion_p,
              field    = betadisper_check(bm$dist, m$field)$dispersion_p)
    #
    perm |> mutate(matrix = label_matrix, 
                   grain = label_grain,
                   n_features = ncol(bm$mat), 
                   dispersion_p = disp[.data$term],
                   skip_reason = NA_character_,
                   .before = 1)}, 
    error = function(e) {
    # if fails, stop.
    message(label_matrix, " grain ", 
            label_grain, " skipped: ", 
            conditionMessage(e))

Definitions - set up for using taxonomic level 4
Same transcripts feed both matrices. Only the column they are summed by changes (taxon vs. ko_id). Three filters make that true and set the unit of analysis:

Shared prep (prep_paired()): Gorda Ridge, Von Damm and Piccard only; no per-row TPM cutoff; transcripts need a lineage and a KO, so the same transcripts count toward both taxonomy and function; Eukaryota-only and Opisthokonta lineages are dropped.

Replicate libraries are averaged to their sample unit (aggregate = "mean" in build_matrix()). Ravelin2, Lotsoshrimp, and Gorda Plume each have two libraries; permuting them as independent samples is pseudoreplication. Every test below runs on sample units.

1. Environmental effects on each matrix

R2 is the fraction of that matrix’s variance explained by the term (marginal test).
If dispersion_p < 0.05, groups differ in spread as well as in centroid, so R² cannot be read as a pure composition difference (Anderson & Walsh 2013).
n_units is the number of sample units. If a vent field has fewer than 3 vent units, the within-vent field test is skipped and that row is absent.



Code
env_effects <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  # Taxonomy
  fit_contrasts(tax$dist, meta, "taxonomy",
                permutations = params$permutations, seed = params$seed),
  # Function
  fit_contrasts(fxn$dist, meta, "function",
                permutations = params$permutations, seed = params$seed)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(contrast, matrix)

env_effects



  



Table interpretation (env_effect):

For the vent vs. non-vent comparison, both the taxonomic and functional profiles separate by habitat. Therefore there is a true difference in composition between vent and non-vent samples.
Once habitat is accounted for, vent field has little effect on either matrix.
The vent-units-only field test is not run: Piccard has 2 vent units, below min_per_field = 3, so that row is absent by design. Do not report a within-vent field R².
Habitat (or sample type) structures both taxonomy and function. Vent field has less of an impact.



2. Is taxonomy structured more than function across the deep-sea vent environment?
Here the question gets its significance test. For each term: ΔR² = R²(taxonomy) − R²(function)
A 95% interval that excludes 0 means the term explains a significantly larger (Δ > 0) or smaller (Δ < 0) share of taxonomic than functional variation.
The interval comes from a delete-one jackknife over sample units (Efron & Stein 1981). Each draw drops one unit and refits both PERMANOVAs. delta_jack is the bias-corrected ΔR² and jack_se its standard error; the CI is centered on delta_jack.
Reading notes:

Each R² is a share of its own matrix’s variance. ΔR² asks which matrix the environment organizes more strongly, not which matrix has more variance.
The two matrices differ in dimensions (grain-4 taxa vs. KOs). The interval captures sampling uncertainty, not that structural difference, so keep the wording at “explains a larger share of variation.”
If a term has heterogeneous dispersion in either matrix (see step 1), its ΔR² mixes centroid and spread differences.

3. Are taxonomy and function coupled? (Procrustes)
Both ordinations are superimposed and the correlation r (0–1) is tested by permutation (Peres-Neto & Jackson 2001). The number of axes is a choice, so we report r at 2–4 axes, along with how much of each matrix’s variation those axes hold. High r means sample units that are taxonomically similar are also functionally similar.
Caveat: both matrices come from the same transcripts, so some shared structure is built in. That makes r an upper bound on biological coupling.


Code
var_captured <- function(d, k) {
  eig <- stats::cmdscale(d, k = attr(d, "Size") - 1, eig = TRUE)$eig
  eig <- eig[eig > 0]
  sum(eig[seq_len(k)]) / sum(eig)
}

coupling <- purrr::map_dfr(2:4, \(k) {
  pt <- procrustes_test(tax$dist, fxn$dist, k = k,
                        permutations = params$permutations, seed = params$seed)
  tibble::tibble(k_axes = k,
                 procrustes_r= pt$t0,
                 p = pt$signif,
                 tax_var_captured = var_captured(tax$dist, k),
                 fxn_var_captured = var_captured(fxn$dist, k))
})

coupling



  




For results — Procrustes r, p and variance captured at k = 2–4 from 04_procrustes.csv.


3b. Is coupling more than a shared response to habitat?
Procrustes r is highest on the first two axes and falls as axes are added. Those leading axes likely carry the vent/non-vent split, so high r could mean only that both matrices separate by habitat. Two checks remove habitat from the comparison:

Vent units only. Within one habitat, habitat cannot drive the match.
Habitat removed. Each unit’s rclr profile is centered on its habitat mean before distances are computed. This is the Euclidean equivalent of partialling vent_bin out of a dbRDA on the robust Aitchison distance (Legendre & Anderson 1999).

Reading notes:

If r stays high and significant in both checks, taxonomy and function are coupled beyond their shared habitat response.
If r drops toward the permutation null, the coupling in step 3 is the habitat signal seen twice.
The vent-only test has fewer units, so its p is less powerful; compare r values, not just significance.

# Procrustes r at k axes for one pair of distance matrices (one row per k)
coupling_at_k <- function(d_tax, d_fxn, test_label, ks = 2:4) {
  purrr::map_dfr(ks, \(k) {
    pt <- procrustes_test(d_tax, d_fxn, k = k,
                          permutations = params$permutations, seed = params$seed)
    tibble::tibble(test = test_label, k_axes = k,
                   procrustes_r = pt$t0, p = pt$signif,
                   n_units = attr(d_tax, "Size"))
  })
}

Which taxonomic and functional profiles track with the vent environment?

Unconstrained. PCoA of the same distances with environmental vectors fitted afterwards (envfit), so the axis percentages describe total among-vent variation and cannot overstate how much of the community the environment explains.
Functional investment. Having established that environment structures the community, which broad functional categories shift with it? Using COG functional categories, KEGG categories, and pfam IDs.

Run dbRDA
Does environment structure taxonomy, function, or both?
For each level, the full model parameters that passed collinearity test, its global test, forward selection (only if the global test passes), and a per-variable table with and without field partialled out.
Constrained ordination (dbRDA) using robust Aitchison distance. This will model the impact of an explanatory matrix (environemtal factors) on a dependent (or response) matrix (TPM results). Oridinate matrix Y (which is the TPM results, the community response) to see what ordination axes are linear combinations of those from X (environmental matrix).


Code
fit_env_dbrda <- function(d, env, vars, n_perm = N_PERM_MODEL) {
  env <- env[match(labels(d), env$unit), ]
  stopifnot(identical(env$unit, labels(d)))
  # Set up dbRDAs
  ## Uses temp, pH and Mg, full model
  full <- vegan::dbrda(stats::reformulate(vars, response = "d"), data = env)
  ## establish start point for forward selection model
  null <- vegan::dbrda(d ~ 1, data = env)
  ## permuration test, rows via n_perm. If p < 0.05, forward selection will run.
  global <- vegan::anova.cca(full, permutations = n_perm)
  #
  ## If the full model using temp, pH, and Mg is significant, then a global model will be run. Otherwise, fall back.
  sel <- if (global$`Pr(>F)`[1] <= 0.05) {
    vegan::ordiR2step(null, scope = stats::formula(full), R2scope = TRUE,
                      permutations = n_perm, trace = FALSE)
  } else null
  selected <- setdiff(all.vars(stats::formula(sel)), "d")

  # Blanchet's second stopping rule rejects any step when adj R2 exceeds the global model. 
  ## Only 1 may be returned,  so selection returns nothing even though the global test passed. If significant, it is significant. use that.
  best_single <- NA_character_
  if (global$`Pr(>F)`[1] <= 0.05 && length(selected) == 0) {
    single_r2 <- purrr::map_dbl(vars, \(v) vegan::RsquareAdj(
      vegan::dbrda(stats::reformulate(v, response = "d"), data = env))$adj.r.squared)
    best_single <- vars[which.max(single_r2)]
    best_model  <- vegan::dbrda(stats::reformulate(best_single, response = "d"), data = env)
    if (vegan::anova.cca(best_model, permutations = n_perm)$`Pr(>F)`[1] <= 0.05) {
      sel <- best_model; selected <- best_single
      message(glue::glue("  {best_single} alone (adj R2 = {round(max(single_r2), 3)}) ",
                         "exceeds the global model; kept as the single selected variable."))
    }
  }

  # Each variable alone, then the same variable after removing field.
  per_var <- purrr::map_dfr(vars, function(v) {
    alone <- vegan::dbrda(stats::reformulate(v, response = "d"), data = env)
    cond <- vegan::dbrda(stats::as.formula(paste("d ~", v, "+ Condition(field)")),
                          data = env)
    tibble::tibble(
      variable = v,
      adjR2_alone = vegan::RsquareAdj(alone)$adj.r.squared,
      p_alone= vegan::anova.cca(alone, permutations = n_perm)$`Pr(>F)`[1],
      adjR2_given_field = vegan::RsquareAdj(cond)$adj.r.squared,
      p_given_field = vegan::anova.cca(cond, permutations = n_perm)$`Pr(>F)`[1])
  })

  list(full = full, selected_model = sel, selected = selected,
       global_F = global$F[1], global_p = global$`Pr(>F)`[1],
       full_adjR2 = vegan::RsquareAdj(full)$adj.r.squared,
       per_var = per_var)
}

 # Get data to work with, vectors, then sites

text:
Functional category composition along the vent gradient
Which functional categories shift in share of expression along the vent gradient? Each COG category’s rclr share across the 13 vent units is rank-correlated (Spearman, permutation p) with each retained environmental variable, and all category x variable tests are BH-corrected as one family. The same scan on KEGG BRITE level-B categories, an independent annotation of the same transcripts, is the check on any COG hit. One association clears BH: amino acid transport and metabolism (COG E) takes a larger share of expression at higher temperature, and KEGG Amino acid metabolism moves the same way. Temperature, Mg and pH all trace the hydrothermal fluid fraction, so the weaker E correlations with Mg and pH are the same signal, not separate results. With 13 units this is exploratory, and “larger share” means a larger fraction of expression, not more transcripts per cell.

spearman_perm <- function(z, x, n_perm = N_PERM_CAT) {
  stopifnot(nrow(z) == length(x))
  # a category with the same value in every unit has no ranks to correlate
  keep <- apply(z, 2, \(col) stats::sd(col) > 0)
  if (any(!keep)) {
    message(glue::glue("  dropped {sum(!keep)} zero-variance feature(s): ",
                       "{paste(colnames(z)[!keep], collapse = ', ')}"))
  }
  z <- z[, keep, drop = FALSE]
  if (ncol(z) == 0) stop("No variable features left to correlate.", call. = FALSE)

  rz  <- scale(apply(z, 2, rank))
  rx  <- as.numeric(scale(rank(x)))
  n   <- length(x)
  rho <- as.vector(crossprod(rz, rx)) / (n - 1)

  perm <- replicate(n_perm, sample(rx))         # units x n_perm
  null <- abs(crossprod(rz, perm)) / (n - 1)     # features x n_perm
  tibble::tibble(feature = colnames(z),
                 rho     = rho,
                 p_perm  = (1 + rowSums(null >= abs(rho))) / (1 + n_perm))
}



COG scan
A transcript with several COG letters (e.g. "BDLTU") splits its scaledTPM equally across them. Categories are summed per biological unit (sum / n_reps) and the units x category matrix is rclr-transformed. All 26 categories are kept, including R and S, because the CLR reference needs the whole composition.


Code
if (!"COG_category" %in% names(paired_mod)) {
  stop("`COG_category` is not in the annotation table. This section needs the eggNOG ",
       "COG column carried from long_frenemies_annot_tax.", call. = FALSE)
}
# transcript id for the support counts; fall back to counting rows
TX_ID <- c("SEQ_ID", "SequenceID")[c("SEQ_ID", "SequenceID") %in% names(paired_mod)][1]

cog_split <- paired_mod |>
  filter(vent_bin == "Vent", !is.na(COG_category), !COG_category %in% c("", "-")) |>
  mutate(.txid = if (!is.na(TX_ID)) .data[[TX_ID]] else row_number(),
         n_cog = nchar(COG_category)) |>
  separate_longer_position(COG_category, width = 1) |>
  rename(cog = COG_category) |>
  mutate(scaledTPM = scaledTPM / n_cog)

cog_mat <- cog_split |>
  group_by(unit = .data[[UNIT_COL]], n_reps, cog) |>
  summarise(tpm = sum(scaledTPM) / first(n_reps), .groups = "drop") |>
  select(-n_reps) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = cog, values_from = tpm, values_fill = 0) |>
  tibble::column_to_rownames("unit") |>
  as.matrix()
cog_mat <- cog_mat[env_model$unit, , drop = FALSE]   # align rows to the dbRDA predictors
cog_z   <- rclr_transform(cog_mat)

cog_support <- cog_split |>
  summarise(n_transcripts = n_distinct(.txid), n_kos = n_distinct(ko_id),
            total_tpm = sum(scaledTPM), .by = cog) |>
  mutate(pct_tpm = round(100 * total_tpm / sum(total_tpm), 2),
         description = unname(COG_DESCRIPTIONS[cog])) |>
  arrange(desc(total_tpm))

set.seed(params$seed)
cog_gradient <- purrr::map_dfr(env_keep, \(v)
  spearman_perm(cog_z, env_model[[v]]) |> mutate(variable = v, .before = 1)) |>
  rename(cog = feature) |>
  mutate(q_bh = stats::p.adjust(p_perm, method = "BH")) |>   # one family: every category x variable
  left_join(select(cog_support, cog, description, n_kos, n_transcripts, pct_tpm), by = "cog") |>
  mutate(direction   = if_else(rho < 0, "decreases", "increases"),
         significant = q_bh <= params$fdr_alpha) |>
  arrange(q_bh)

message(glue::glue("{nrow(cog_mat)} vent units x {ncol(cog_mat)} COG categories; ",
                   "{sum(cog_gradient$significant)} of {nrow(cog_gradient)} tests clear BH q <= {params$fdr_alpha}"))


13 vent units x 24 COG categories; 1 of 72 tests clear BH q <= 0.05




KEGG check
Same build with KEGG BRITE level-B categories. A KO in n level-B categories splits its scaledTPM equally across them; KOs with no retained category drop out, so the composition is over mapped expression only.


Code
if (!file.exists(KEGG_BRITE_FILE)) {
  stop("`", KEGG_BRITE_FILE, "` not found. Download the KEGG BRITE KO hierarchy once, e.g.\n",
       "  curl -o ", KEGG_BRITE_FILE, " \"https://rest.kegg.jp/get/br:ko00001\"\n",
       "then re-run.", call. = FALSE)
}
# >SKH: shared parser R/read_brite.R (same map 05, 05b and 06 use; 2026-10-12)
brite_map <- read_brite_level_b(KEGG_BRITE_FILE, exclude_a = KEGG_EXCLUDE_A) |>
  select(ko_id, kegg_a, kegg, description, n_cat)

kegg_split <- paired_mod |>
  filter(vent_bin == "Vent") |>
  transmute(unit = .data[[UNIT_COL]], n_reps, ko_id, scaledTPM,
            .txid = if (!is.na(TX_ID)) .data[[TX_ID]] else row_number()) |>
  inner_join(brite_map, by = "ko_id", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  mutate(scaledTPM = scaledTPM / n_cat)

# mass conservation: splitting across categories must not create or lose TPM
vent_ko_tpm <- paired_mod |> filter(vent_bin == "Vent")
mapped_tpm  <- sum(vent_ko_tpm$scaledTPM[vent_ko_tpm$ko_id %in% brite_map$ko_id])
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(kegg_split$scaledTPM), mapped_tpm)))

kegg_mat <- kegg_split |>
  summarise(tpm = sum(scaledTPM) / first(n_reps), .by = c(unit, n_reps, kegg)) |>
  select(-n_reps) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = kegg, values_from = tpm, values_fill = 0) |>
  tibble::column_to_rownames("unit") |>
  as.matrix()
kegg_mat <- kegg_mat[env_model$unit, , drop = FALSE]
kegg_z   <- rclr_transform(kegg_mat)

kegg_support <- kegg_split |>
  summarise(n_transcripts = n_distinct(.txid), n_kos = n_distinct(ko_id),
            total_tpm = sum(scaledTPM), .by = c(kegg, description)) |>
  mutate(pct_tpm = round(100 * total_tpm / sum(total_tpm), 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(total_tpm))

set.seed(params$seed)
kegg_gradient <- purrr::map_dfr(env_keep, \(v)
  spearman_perm(kegg_z, env_model[[v]]) |> mutate(variable = v, .before = 1)) |>
  rename(kegg = feature) |>
  mutate(q_bh = stats::p.adjust(p_perm, method = "BH")) |>
  left_join(select(kegg_support, kegg, description, n_kos, n_transcripts, pct_tpm), by = "kegg") |>
  mutate(direction   = if_else(rho < 0, "decreases", "increases"),
         significant = q_bh <= params$fdr_alpha) |>
  arrange(q_bh)

message(glue::glue(
  "{round(100 * mapped_tpm / sum(vent_ko_tpm$scaledTPM), 1)}% of vent KO TPM maps to a KEGG level-B category; ",
  "{sum(kegg_gradient$significant)} of {nrow(kegg_gradient)} tests clear BH q <= {params$fdr_alpha}"))

if (top_cog$cog != FOCUS_COG || top_cog$variable != FOCUS_VAR) {

title: 04 — Taxonomy vs. function across habitats and the vent environment
text:
Where this goes next
04 asks how environment structures the vent protist community (dbRDA and envfit above), then scans functional category composition against the same gradient (exploratory). The pre-specified growth test (translation, folding, energy categories) was removed on 2026-10-13; see scripts/ARCHIVE/ARCHIVE_05_growth_apriori.qmd.
What 04 deliberately does not answer is which taxa carry the signal. At 13 vent units a single-feature test has almost no power, and the one feature that survived family-wise correction could not support an interpretation. 06 takes the same vent units and asks the taxon-level question with more data behind each claim: how broadly across vent-associated taxa each KO is expressed, and whether the curated heterotrophy KOs sit at the lineage-restricted or the broadly shared end of that distribution.

title: 06b — Trophic signatures in protist lineages
text:
Lineage groups
Fixed before looking at the data, from the literature; edit lineage_groups to change membership. Each contrast compares lineages with a documented lifestyle (focal) against free-living relatives in the same phylum (reference). Lineages not listed (e.g. “(unres.)” bins, Mesodinium) stay out of both sides.

Ciliates. Armophorea, Muranotrichea and Parablepharismea form a clade of obligate anaerobes that all host prokaryotic symbionts (Rotterová et al. 2020, Curr Biol 30:2037–2050); Plagiopylea are anaerobic ciliates with prokaryotic symbionts (Fenchel et al. 1977, J Protozool 24:154–163), including a denitrifying endosymbiont (Graf et al. 2021, Nature 591:445–450).
Syndiniales. Parasitoids of other protists (John et al. 2019, Sci Adv 5:eaav1110; Farhat et al. 2018, Front Microbiol 9:2251), against free-living dinoflagellate lineages. Dinophyceae includes mixotrophs and a few parasites, so the reference is not purely free-living.
Myzozoa. Apicomplexans, gregarines, squirmids and perkinsids (parasites) against chromerids and colpodellids (free-living photosynthetic or predatory relatives; Woo et al. 2015, eLife 4:e06974; Mathur et al. 2019, Curr Biol 29:2936–2941; Leander et al. 2003, J Eukaryot Microbiol 50:334–340; Hoppenrath and Leander 2009, J Eukaryot Microbiol 56:251–256).


SKH:

                       "Oligohymenophorea", "Phyllopharyngea", "Prostomatea", "Spirotrichea")
myzozoa_parasite  <- c("Aconoidasia", "Apicomplexa (unres.)", "Ancora", "Cardiosporidium",
                       "Cephaloidophora", "Digyalum", "Eleutheroschizon", "Filipodium",
                       "Hammondia", "Lankesteria", "Platyproteum", "Polyplicarium",
                       "Rhytidocystis", "Selenidium", "Siedleckia", "Squirmida (unres.)",
                       "Perkinsea (unres.)", "Perkinsida")
myzozoa_freeliving <- c("Alphamonadaceae", "Chromeraceae", "Chromerida_X", "Colpodellaceae",
                        "Colpodellida (unres.)", "Colponema", "Colponemidia (unres.)",
                        "Vitrellaceae")

lineage_groups <- bind_rows(
  tibble(contrast = "Ciliates: anaerobic, symbiont-bearing vs. other classes",
         phylum = "Alveolata-Ciliophora", role = "focal",
         lineage = c("Armophorea", "Muranotrichea", "Parablepharismea", "Plagiopylea")),
  tibble(contrast = "Ciliates: anaerobic, symbiont-bearing vs. other classes",
         phylum = "Alveolata-Ciliophora", role = "reference", lineage = ciliate_reference),
  # Syndiniales: every lineage of the curated Syndiniales phylum, plus Amoebophryaceae
  # wherever the curation placed it
  pairs |> filter(phylum == "Alveolata-Syndiniales") |> distinct(phylum, lineage) |>
    mutate(contrast = "Syndiniales vs. free-living dinoflagellates", role = "focal"),
  tibble(contrast = "Syndiniales vs. free-living dinoflagellates",
         phylum = "Alveolata-Dinophyta", role = "focal", lineage = "Amoebophryaceae"),
  tibble(contrast = "Syndiniales vs. free-living dinoflagellates",
         phylum = "Alveolata-Dinophyta", role = "reference",
         lineage = c("Dinophyceae", "Noctilucales", "Oxyrrhinales")),
  tibble(contrast = "Myzozoa: parasites vs. free-living relatives",
         phylum = "Alveolata-Myzozoa", role = "focal", lineage = myzozoa_parasite),
  tibble(contrast = "Myzozoa: parasites vs. free-living relatives",
         phylum = "Alveolata-Myzozoa", role = "reference", lineage = myzozoa_freeliving))

  inner_join(lineage_groups, by = c("phylum", "lineage"), relationship = "many-to-many")

# KO pool per side: union of member lineages, weight = summed scaledTPM
pools <- grouped_pairs |>
  summarise(weight     = pmax(sum(tpm_total), 1e-9),   # a detected pair always counts
            n_lineages = n_distinct(cur_L4), .by = c(contrast, role, ko_id))

pool_sizes <- pools |>
  summarise(n_kos = n_distinct(ko_id), .by = c(contrast, role)) |>
  left_join(grouped_pairs |> summarise(lineages = paste(sort(unique(lineage)), collapse = ", "),

06b — Trophic signatures in protist lineages
text:
Depth-matched comparison
A lineage pool with few detected KOs holds mostly its most highly expressed ones, so a raw “share of the repertoire in set X” mixes biology with sequencing depth. Here both pools are rarefied to the same number of KOs (the smaller pool’s size), drawing KOs without replacement with probability proportional to their summed scaledTPM, which mimics detection at a lower depth. For each set and draw: diff = members in focal − members in reference. Reported per set: median diff, its 2.5–97.5% range over N_RAREFY draws, and frac_focal_higher. This is a rarefaction summary, not a hypothesis test: an interval that excludes 0 means the difference holds at matched depth, nothing more, and with pools of tens of KOs it should be read as exploratory.

rarefied_contrast <- function(pool_focal, pool_ref, sets, n_draws = N_RAREFY) {
  n_draw  <- min(nrow(pool_focal), nrow(pool_ref))
  set_ids <- sets |>
    filter(ko_id %in% c(pool_focal$ko_id, pool_ref$ko_id)) |>
    add_count(set_source, set_name, name = "n_in_pools") |>
    filter(n_in_pools >= MIN_SET_IN_POOL)
  if (!nrow(set_ids) || n_draw < 2) return(tibble())

  # KO x set incidence, so one draw is a single colSums()
  set_keys  <- set_ids |> distinct(set_source, set_name) |>
    mutate(key = paste(set_source, set_name, sep = " :: "))
  all_kos   <- union(pool_focal$ko_id, pool_ref$ko_id)
  incidence <- matrix(0L, length(all_kos), nrow(set_keys),
                      dimnames = list(all_kos, set_keys$key))
  incidence[cbind(set_ids$ko_id, paste(set_ids$set_source, set_ids$set_name, sep = " :: "))] <- 1L

  draw_counts <- function(pool) {
    replicate(n_draws, colSums(incidence[sample(pool$ko_id, n_draw, prob = pool$weight), ,
                                         drop = FALSE]))
  }
  diffs <- matrix(draw_counts(pool_focal) - draw_counts(pool_ref), nrow = nrow(set_keys))

  # member KO ids on each side, so overlap between KEGG maps is visible
  # (the same cathepsin or V-ATPase can sit in Lysosome, Phagocytosis and Apoptosis)
  members_in <- function(pool) {
    map_chr(set_keys$key, \(k) paste(sort(intersect(pool$ko_id, all_kos[incidence[, k] == 1L])),
                                     collapse = " | "))
  }

  set_keys |>
    mutate(n_rarefied        = n_draw,
           in_focal_pool     = colSums(incidence[pool_focal$ko_id, , drop = FALSE]),
           in_ref_pool       = colSums(incidence[pool_ref$ko_id, , drop = FALSE]),
           focal_member_kos  = members_in(pool_focal),
           ref_member_kos    = members_in(pool_ref),
           diff_median       = apply(diffs, 1, median),
           diff_lo           = apply(diffs, 1, quantile, 0.025),
           diff_hi           = apply(diffs, 1, quantile, 0.975),
           frac_focal_higher = rowMeans(diffs > 0),
           frac_ref_higher   = rowMeans(diffs < 0),
           interval_excludes_0 = diff_lo > 0 | diff_hi < 0) |>
    select(-key)
}
